content.value: Think of Git as a supercharged 'Time Machine' for your code. Every time you make a checkpoint (called a **commit**), Git saves a snapshot of your entire project. If you break something, you can easily travel back to any previous snapshot.

It also lets multiple software engineers work on the exact same project simultaneously without overwriting each other's work. Git is a **Distributed Version Control System** (DVCS) — every developer has a full copy of the entire project history on their machine.

Git vs GitHub: Git is the command-line tool running on your computer. GitHub is a cloud website (like Google Drive for code) that hosts Git repositories. Other alternatives include GitLab and Bitbucket.

content.title: First Time Setup
content.value:
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "your.email@example.com"
git init                     # Turn current folder into a Git repository
git status                   # Check what files have changed

quiz.question: What is the primary difference between Git and GitHub?
options: They are the exact same product
Git is the local version control tool; GitHub is a cloud hosting service for Git repos
Git is for Python; GitHub is for JavaScript
GitHub runs on your laptop; Git is a website
quiz.explanation: Git is the underlying tool that tracks file changes locally. GitHub is a cloud platform for storing and sharing Git repositories online.

content.value: Git has a unique concept called the **Staging Area** (also called the Index). Think of it like a photography studio: you don't take a photo of your entire house — you choose which items to arrange on the stage, then take the photo (commit).

content.title: The Three Areas of Git
content.value:
graph LR
    A["📁 Working Directory\n(Your actual files)"] -->|git add| B["📦 Staging Area\n(Ready for snapshot)"]
    B -->|git commit| C["📸 Repository\n(Permanent history)"]
    C -->|git checkout| A
    style A fill:#1a2332,stroke:#ef4444,color:#e2e8f0
    style B fill:#1a2332,stroke:#f59e0b,color:#e2e8f0
    style C fill:#1a2332,stroke:#10b981,color:#e2e8f0

content.title: Staging and Committing
content.value:
# Stage specific files
git add index.html             # Stage one file
git add src/                   # Stage entire directory
git add .                      # Stage ALL changes
git add -p                     # Interactive: choose which changes to stage

# Check what's staged
git status                     # See staged vs unstaged files
git diff                       # See unstaged changes
git diff --staged              # See what's about to be committed

# Commit (take the snapshot)
git commit -m "Add login page"           # Commit with a message
git commit -am "Fix typo"                # Stage + commit tracked files

# Undo mistakes
git restore file.txt                     # Discard unstaged changes
git restore --staged file.txt            # Unstage a file (keep changes)
Good commit messages follow this pattern: 'verb + what changed'. Examples: 'Add user login page', 'Fix database connection timeout', 'Remove deprecated API endpoint'. Bad example: 'fixed stuff'.

quiz.question: What does 'git add' do?
options: Moves files from working directory to the staging area
quiz.explanation: git add moves changes from your Working Directory to the Staging Area. They are now 'staged' and ready to be included in the next commit.

content.value: A **branch** is like a parallel universe for your project. The main production code lives on the `main` branch. When building a new feature, you create a feature branch so you don't break working code. When the feature is done and tested, you merge it back.

content.title: Branch and Merge Workflow
content.value:
gitGraph
    commit id: "Initial"
    commit id: "Setup"
    branch feature-login
    checkout feature-login
    commit id: "Add form"
    commit id: "Add validation"
    checkout main
    commit id: "Hotfix"
    merge feature-login id: "Merge feature"
    commit id: "Deploy v2"

content.title: Branching Commands
content.value:
# Create and manage branches
git branch                      # List all local branches
git branch feature-login        # Create a new branch
git checkout feature-login      # Switch to feature-login branch
git checkout -b feature-login   # Shortcut: create AND switch
git switch feature-login        # Modern alternative to checkout
git switch -c feature-login     # Modern: create AND switch

# Merging
git checkout main               # Switch back to main
git merge feature-login         # Merge feature-login INTO main

# Cleanup
git branch -d feature-login     # Delete branch after merge
git branch -D feature-login     # Force delete unmerged branch
Naming convention: Use descriptive branch names with prefixes. Examples: feature/user-auth, bugfix/login-crash, hotfix/security-patch, chore/update-deps. This makes branches self-documenting.

quiz.question: Why do developers create feature branches instead of committing directly to main?
options: To make the code run faster
To keep working production code safe while developing new features separately
Because Git requires at least 5 branches
quiz.explanation: Feature branches isolate experimental or incomplete work from the stable main codebase until the feature is tested and ready to merge.

content.value: A **merge conflict** happens when two branches modify the same line in the same file. Git doesn't know which version to keep, so it asks YOU to resolve it manually. Don't panic — conflicts are normal and are a sign of active collaboration!

content.title: How Merge Conflicts Happen
content.value:
sequenceDiagram participant M as main participant A as feature-A participant B as feature-B M->>A: Branch off M->>B: Branch off A->>A: Edit line 10: color = blue B->>B: Edit line 10: color = red A->>M: Merge feature-A ✅ B->>M: Merge feature-B ⚠️ CONFLICT! Note over M: Both changed line 10!
Git asks YOU to choose.

content.title: What a Conflict Looks Like in Your File
content.value:
<<<<<<< HEAD (your current branch)
color = blue
=======
color = red
>>>>>>> feature-B (the branch being merged)

# To resolve:
# 1. Choose one version, combine them, or write something new
# 2. Remove the <<<, ===, >>> markers
# 3. Save the file
# 4. git add the resolved file
# 5. git commit to complete the merge

content.title: Conflict Resolution Commands
content.value:
# When a merge conflict occurs:
git status                      # See which files have conflicts

# After manually editing the conflicted file:
git add resolved-file.txt       # Mark as resolved
git commit                      # Complete the merge

# Abort if you want to start over:
git merge --abort               # Cancel the merge entirely

# Use a visual merge tool:
git mergetool                   # Opens configured visual diff tool

Interview pro tip: 'I minimize conflicts by keeping feature branches short-lived (merge within 1-2 days), frequently pulling from main to stay updated, and communicating with teammates when we're working on the same files.'

quiz.question: What causes a Git merge conflict?
options: Two branches modifying the same line in the same file
quiz.explanation: Conflicts occur when Git can't automatically merge because two branches changed the same lines. You must manually choose which changes to keep.

content.value: Both `merge` and `rebase` combine work from two branches, but they do it differently. This is one of the most frequently asked Git questions in interviews.

content.title: Merge: Preserves Full History
content.value:
gitGraph
    commit id: "A"
    commit id: "B"
    branch feature
    checkout feature
    commit id: "C"
    commit id: "D"
    checkout main
    commit id: "E"
    merge feature id: "Merge commit"

**Merge** creates a new 'merge commit' that ties both branches together. The history shows exactly when and where the branch diverged and reconnected. It's safe and preserves the full truth of what happened.

**Rebase** replays your feature commits on top of the latest main, creating a clean linear history as if you had started your work from the latest main all along. The history looks cleaner, but it rewrites commit hashes.

content.title: When to Use Each
content.value:
# MERGE — Safe for shared/public branches
git checkout main
git merge feature-login         # Creates a merge commit

# REBASE — Clean history for local/private branches
git checkout feature-login
git rebase main                 # Replay commits on top of main
git checkout main
git merge feature-login         # Now it's a fast-forward (linear)

# Interactive rebase — Squash messy commits before merge
git rebase -i HEAD~3            # Rewrite last 3 commits
# In the editor: change 'pick' to 'squash' to combine commits

Golden Rule: NEVER rebase commits that have been pushed to a shared branch that others are working on. Rebase rewrites commit history, which will cause chaos for teammates who already have the old commits. Only rebase your own local, unpushed work.

quiz.question: When is it safe to use git rebase?
options: Only on your local, unpushed feature branches
quiz.explanation: Rebase rewrites commit history. It's safe on local branches that haven't been shared. Never rebase commits already pushed to shared branches — it creates duplicate commits for teammates.

content.value: **Git Stash** is like a clipboard for your code changes. Imagine you're halfway through writing a feature, and your boss says 'Drop everything — fix this critical bug on main!' Stash saves your unfinished work, lets you switch branches cleanly, and restores it later.

content.title: Git Stash — Save Work in Progress
content.value:
# Save current changes to stash
git stash                       # Stash tracked file changes
git stash -u                    # Also stash untracked (new) files
git stash save "WIP: login form"  # Stash with a description

# View and restore stashed changes
git stash list                  # List all stashes
git stash pop                   # Restore most recent stash & remove from list
git stash apply                 # Restore stash but keep it in the list
git stash drop stash@{0}        # Delete a specific stash
git stash clear                 # Delete ALL stashes
**Git Tags** mark specific commits as important milestones — like software version releases (v1.0.0, v2.3.1). Tags don't move like branches do; they permanently point to one specific commit.

content.title: Git Tags — Version Marking
content.value:
git tag v1.0.0                  # Create a lightweight tag
git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "First stable release"  # Annotated tag (recommended)
git tag                         # List all tags
git push origin v1.0.0          # Push a specific tag to remote
git push origin --tags          # Push ALL tags to remote

content.title: Git Log — Explore History
content.value:
git log                         # Full commit history
git log --oneline               # Compact one-line format
git log --oneline --graph       # Visual branch graph
git log --author="Alice"        # Filter by author
git log --since="2 weeks ago"   # Filter by date
git show abc1234                # Show details of a specific commit
git blame file.txt              # Show who last modified each line
git blame is incredibly useful for debugging: 'Who changed this line, when, and in which commit?' It helps you find the context behind a change before you modify it.

quiz.question: When would you use git stash?
options: To temporarily save uncommitted changes so you can switch branches
quiz.explanation: Git stash temporarily shelves your uncommitted changes so you can work on something else (like a hotfix on another branch), then restore your work later with git stash pop.

sections.title: GitHub Pull Requests and Code Review

content.value: A **Pull Request** (PR) is how teams collaborate on GitHub. Instead of pushing directly to main, you push your feature branch and open a PR asking teammates to review your code before merging. Think of it as submitting a homework assignment for your professor to grade before it counts.

content.title: Pull Request Workflow
content.value:
sequenceDiagram
    participant D as Developer
    participant GH as GitHub
    participant R as Code Reviewer
    D->>D: Create feature branch
    D->>D: Write code + commit
    D->>GH: git push origin feature-branch
    D->>GH: Open Pull Request
    GH->>R: Notification: PR ready for review
    R->>GH: Review code + leave comments
    R->>GH: Request changes ❌
    D->>D: Fix issues + push updates
    R->>GH: Approve ✅
    GH->>GH: Merge to main
    GH->>GH: Delete feature branch

content.title: PR Workflow from Command Line
content.value:
# 1. Create and switch to feature branch
git checkout -b feature/user-profile

# 2. Make changes, commit
git add .
git commit -m "Add user profile page with avatar upload"

# 3. Push branch to GitHub
git push origin feature/user-profile

# 4. Open PR on GitHub (or use GitHub CLI)
gh pr create --title "Add user profile page" --body "Implements user profile with avatar upload."

# 5. After PR is approved and merged, clean up
git checkout main
git pull origin main             # Get the merged changes
git branch -d feature/user-profile  # Delete local branch

Code review best practices: Keep PRs small (under 400 lines), write descriptive PR titles and descriptions, add screenshots for UI changes, respond to review comments promptly, and test before requesting review.

content.title: Keeping Your Branch Updated
content.value:
# While working on a feature, main may get new commits
# Keep your branch updated to avoid conflicts:
git checkout feature/user-profile
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main           # Replay your commits on latest main

# Or merge main into your branch:
git merge origin/main            # Merge latest main into your branch

quiz.question: Why do teams use Pull Requests instead of pushing directly to main?
options: To allow code review, catch bugs, and ensure code quality before merging
Because git push doesn't work on main
quiz.explanation: Pull Requests enable peer code review, which catches bugs, improves code quality, shares knowledge across the team, and creates a documented discussion trail for each change.
